title: The Fabulous Dorseys jam session with Art Tatum
summary: He recalls the nightclub jam scene with Tatum, Ziggy Elman and the Dorseys where the booze was real.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: Then we have, "The Fabulous Dorseys," 1947, 87 minutes, directed by Alfred E. Green. Dull cliche biography of the two brothers played by themselves with a weighty selection of musical items from their repertoire, including, "Marie," "Green Eyes," "Never Say Never," "The Object of My Affections," and "Dorothy Concerto," by Leo Schuken, and Ray Bauduc. Both the Jimmy Dorsey Orchestra and the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra, with Alvin Stoller on drums, appear with guests Ray Eberle, Stuart Foster, Mike Pingatore, Helen O'Connell, Henry Busse and Paul Whiteman. The only high spot is a jam session sequence featuring Art Tatum piano, Charlie Barnet, alto sax, Ziggy Elman, trumpet, Tommy Dorsey, trombone, Jimmy Dorsey, clarinet, Ray Bauduc, drums, plus bass and guitar, with "Art's Blues."

Oh, yeah. It was a nightclub scene, and at that time the Old Grey Fox, was what we used to call Tommy then, was on the wagon. He wasn't drinking. But everybody else was. All the booze on the tables in the nightclub scene was real. And we had a delightful time there.
Sounds like it must have been a great
jam session. I don't think I ever saw the film. Tatum on piano.
Yeah. It shows up every once in awhile on one of the late, late shows.
